extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, and media-literacy researchers seeking information on a specific fake-news/satire website
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria and indicators to judge or describe an online site that publishes fabricated or satirical news (using the National Report article as the source example). Useful for media-literacy, fact-checking, and journalistic vetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictional content
rubrics_metrics.description: Posts fictional articles related to world events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states National Report "posts fictional articles related to world events." This is the primary content characteristic: articles are not factual news but fabricated fiction. The site itself provides a disclaimer that its content is fiction (see related criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-description and disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: The National Report describes itself as a "news and political satire web publication" and provides a disclaimer that "all news articles contained within National Report are fiction".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-labelling as satire/fake and an explicit disclaimer are indicators the publisher presents itself as non-factual. The page notes the existence of this disclaimer and quotes its wording directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer prominence / visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: No prominent link to [the disclaimer] page was seen until late December 2014.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a site carries a disclaimer, the prominence and discoverability of that disclaimer matter: an obscure or hard-to-find disclaimer increases the risk that readers will interpret stories as factual. The article highlights the late appearance of a prominent disclaimer link as a problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: External characterization by fact-checkers and press
rubrics_metrics.description: Described by Snopes.com as a fake news site, by FactCheck.org as a satirical site, and by The Washington Post as part of a fake-news industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How independent fact-checkers and reputable press outlets categorize the site is a key external credibility signal. Multiple third-party labels (fake news, satire, part of a fake-news industry) provide corroborating evidence about the site's nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform labeling / intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: A Facebook interface experiment included the site on a list of those whose stories were flagged as 'satire' when appearing on the social network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform-driven flags, labels, or UI treatments (e.g., 'satire' tags) are relevant indicators of how major distribution platforms view and treat the site's content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation: profit-driven vs satirical intent
rubrics_metrics.description: "Not driven by trying to do comedy or satire, but by what kind of fake stuff can we spin up to get shares that earn us money,"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported motivations affect evaluation: a site driven primarily by generating shares and ad revenue (rather than producing bona fide satire or commentary) suggests an intent to mislead for profit. The article cites Craig Silverman's characterization of National Report's motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization capability / advertising incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularly widely spread hoax stories [are] capable of earning thousands of dollars per day from on-site advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of on-site advertising and demonstrated ability to monetize viral hoaxes is an evaluative dimension: high monetization potential creates incentives to produce misleading content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virality and engagement versus corrective coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories led to large traffic spikes — e.g., a traffic spike of two million unique visitors — and the original National Report story received six times as many 'shares' on social media sites as the debunking stories did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare engagement metrics (shares, unique visitors) for the false story versus debunking coverage. High virality of the hoax relative to corrections indicates greater real-world spread and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track record of being mistaken as factual by media
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories from the National Report have been taken seriously by third parties such as Fox News Channel; several hoax stories have been mistakenly reported as fact by media outlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A history of mainstream media or other authorities treating the site's stories as factual is an important indicator of a site's capacity to mislead and cause misinformation incidents. The article gives examples (Fox News, other outlets) and specific stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-world harms and international incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: A report claiming a fictitious Assam Rape Festival created a furor in Indian national and local media; a police probe showed the story originated from Uganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented consequences — public outrage, international incidents, police probes — show the potential harms of fabricated stories. Evaluators should note both domestic and international impacts of hoaxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and ownership transparency (pseudonyms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Owner Jestin Coler (also known as Allen Montgomery); Paul Horner was the publication's lead writer; Coler wrote under the pseudonym 'Allen Montgomery.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency about ownership and authorship — or use of pseudonyms — affects credibility assessments. Pseudonymous writing and opaque ownership can be a red flag for accountability and editorial standards.
